extracted.intended_audience: school principals, teachers, and administrators (particularly of girls' academies)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for organizing and managing the daily schedule, instructional structure, officer roles, pupil supervision (classes and sections), minor-discipline court, and religious/moral instruction in a school. Focused on operational procedures and duties of teachers and student officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timekeeping and signaling (bells and Study Card)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bell is always rung five minutes before the time for closing the recitation, to give the teachers notice that their time is nearly expired, and then again at the time, to give notice to new classes to take their places. At the end of the first hour, the Study Card will be let half down, five minutes, and its bell is the signal for universal permission to whisper and to leave seats (not for loud talking or play). When the five minutes has expired, the Card goes up again, and its sound immediately restores silence and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise advance and final signals structure class transitions and recesses. Use half-drop for brief permitted relaxation (whispering/leaving seats), full drop for recess/greater change. Ringing one minute before end of General Exercise and recess is also advised. Maintain consistency so pupils learn expected behaviour on each signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide hours into halves with fixed recitation periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Each study hour is divided into two equal parts; some classes recite in the first part, and others in the second. The bell is rung at the close of each half hour and five minutes before the close to give notice that recitation time is about to expire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling many small recitation groups across the first three hours allows every pupil to be employed according to parent wishes, health, and ability. Use posted lists showing class times and teachers so pupils can plan; encourage pupils to mark study and recitation times on their schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Exercise quarter (purpose and management)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quarter of an hour marked G (General Exercise) when each pupil lays aside her work and attends to proposed exercises. Purposes include short lectures on useful subjects, general reading lessons, Bible class, or attending to general business of the school. The bell is rung one minute before the close; when it expires the Study Card is let entirely down and the room becomes lively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this flexible fifteen-minute block for variety: moral instruction, reading, communal business, or short lectures. Keep it brief, signal one minute before end to restore order; it is also the time when pupils may express suggestions through the school’s business procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess structure and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Recess is a quarter of an hour marked R. Amusements include battledoors, soft balls, marching to piano with whistle signals. One minute before it expires the bell is rung to signal preparation to return; when the Study Card goes up silence and order are restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep recess short and structured to avoid crowding and tardiness on return. Use whistle signals and arranged amusements; plan ingress/egress to avoid congestion. Supervision and modest rules prevent noisy disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and conduct of classes (instructional aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of dividing pupils into classes is instruction. The manner of recitation is varied; the design is not to have you commit to memory what the book contains, but to understand and digest it—to incorporate it into your mind. Do not endeavor to fix words, but ideas. Conceive clearly, paint distinctly, contemplate facts in their relations, exercising judgment and reasoning rather than mere memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should focus recitations on comprehension and critical thinking rather than rote memorization. Encourage imaginative and relational understanding; vary recitation methods; expect pupils to prepare lessons but allow flexibility in when they prepare them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedules and pupil workload management
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of classes, average age, teacher, and time is posted. Scholars prepare lessons when they please and are expected to be present and prepared at recitation time. Teachers must examine pleas of lack of time to ascertain whether a pupil has joined too many classes and adjust assignments so each pupil has sufficient in-school occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage pupils to reflect on their course load and consult principal/parents about changes. Teachers should actively help rebalance workloads to prevent chronic unpreparedness; promote systematic scheduling (mark study and recitation times) to regulate each pupil's time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into Sections for supervision (not instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the last hour pupils are divided into six sections (by age/maturity) under Superintendents for supervision rather than instruction. Sections attend to administration: supplying materials, arranging work, assisting new pupils, correcting faults, and generally promoting welfare and progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sections to address pupils' non-instructional needs and character development. Sections may have their own officers and plans; Superintendents should use section meetings for moral/religious subjects, compositions, or discussions. Allow sections latitude but require records and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of a Superintendent (enumerated responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Prepare an exact list of members and become intimately acquainted with them; 2) Superintend the preparation of their schedules—ensure enough but not too much work and report needed changes to the principal; 3) Supply daily wants—pens, paper, desks—and help new scholars find companions; 4) Watch characters of members—inquiring of teachers about progress, punctuality, desk neatness, and correcting or referring cases; 5) Secure progress in essential studies (reading, writing, spelling) without letting instruction interfere with superintendent duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superintendents must exert personal influence, keep faithful records of plans and history, and act as if the section were a separate school. They should not make major changes without consulting the principal; their role is supervision—'seeing that a thing is done'—not unilateral reassignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Superintendent authority and collaborative problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Superintendents ought not to make changes, except in very plain cases, without referring the subject to the principal. They should not assume either full responsibility outside their authority or neglect cases because they lack formal power; e.g., if a pupil is in too high an arithmetic class the Superintendent should consult the teacher, find a suitable class, then present facts to the principal for decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize procedural referral and cooperative resolution. Superintendents should use persuasion, inquiry, and documented recommendation rather than unilateral action when remedying misassignments or other systemic issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student officers and five departments of business
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five departments entrusted to student officers: 1) Regulators—to assist in routine business (ringing bells, managing study card, distributing/collecting papers, counting votes); 2) Secretaries—keeping records and executing writing; 3) Accountants—keeping register of scholars and accounts; 4) Librarians—to take charge of books and stationery; 5) Curators—to secure neatness and order in apartments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign specific, repeatable duties to student officers to divide labor and build responsibility. Departments should meet, keep records, and plan for efficiency. Tailor detailed duties to the particular school; maintain teacher oversight for appointments and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer selection and eligibility rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretaries and Accountants are appointed by the Principal (usually chosen from teachers). The first in each other department are chosen by ballot by the scholars; each nominates assistants whose nominations must be approved at a teacher's meeting. No person may hold office in two departments; officers inattentive or disorderly should not be appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine democratic selection with teacher/principal vetting to ensure competent student leadership. Use teacher oversight to prevent unfit appointments and to approve nominations for assistants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor example and practical procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Example procedure: issue order at business quarter hour for distributors to place a piece of paper on each desk; collectors gather papers, deliver them to Accountants who copy them into a prepared book, arranging alphabetically; the writer copies fairly. This division of labor speeds administrative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small, concrete tasks assigned to appropriate departments to accomplish administrative needs quickly. Define stepwise procedures and a clear chain of custody (who collects, who receives, who records) to avoid duplication and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment and accountability for officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Any scholar may propose the impeachment of an officer who is partial, unfaithful, or negligent. After hearing the officer's written defence, a vote is taken on sustaining the impeachment; if sustained, she is deprived of office and another appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a transparent corrective mechanism to maintain officer accountability. Ensure a fair hearing and allow democratic removal subject to both student participation and teacher oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Court for minor misdemeanors (process and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor transgressions relating chiefly to order are tried by a court (half in jest, half in earnest). Procedure: an indictment is prepared; witnesses named; notice given; an appointed sheriff summons accused and witnesses; a precinct is marked off; jurors are appointed; testimony and defence are heard; jury returns guilty/not guilty. Sentences are slight and real (confinement to seat during a recess or similar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a light-weight, ritualized court to correct recurrent minor misbehaviour and to amuse while preserving order. Keep penalties small but consequential. Make the procedure public and educational rather than purely punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping and colors for section materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section keeps records and uses a color scheme: senior sections use light blue paper, middle sections light straw color, junior sections pink for schedules and records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize stationery and records by section to aid organization and identification. Require Superintendents to keep careful records of plans and section histories to support continuity and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and moral instruction as a central school aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The school intends to exert a decided moral and religious influence. The principal should try to win pupils to piety and create an atmosphere where conscience, moral principle, and affection for God prevail. The aim is pupils becoming sincere and practical Christians, as this promotes obedience, success in study, happiness, and future prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make moral and religious influence frank, open, and decided but gentle and alluring rather than reliant on prizes or threats. Integrate moral topics into section meetings, compositions, and general exercises; consult with parents and respect denominational variety while maintaining clear moral aims.
